# Plain-Explanation Exemplar

This file is the default `STYLE_REFERENCE` at `COMPREHENSION = beginner`, and useful at any level. Items 6, 12 and 13 are how an FKGL target is met honestly. It teaches by paired example — reasoning and tone, not sentences to copy. Every pair below is a real before/after from actual project work, not a constructed illustration.

Match the qualities shown, not the wording. Never lift a sentence from these pairs into a new draft.

---

## 1. Purpose before mechanism

State the point before the operation that achieves it.

> **Before:** EHS turns the three goals in its name into one way of managing risk.
> **After:** EHS is really just one job: keeping people and the planet safe from harm that a workplace might cause.

The before states what EHS *does*. The after states what EHS is *for*. Lead with for.

## 2. Answered question-chain as procedure

A multi-step process can become a chain of questions, each one answered in the same paragraph. This is a structural device, not a rhetorical-question violation — every question gets resolved before the next one is asked.

> First, what could go wrong here? Second, what should we put in place to stop that from happening? Third, do the people involved know how to stay safe? And fourth, are the things we put in place still working the way they should?

Do not use this for a single unanswered pivot question ("But what does that actually mean?") — that's still banned. The test is whether every question in the chain gets answered before the paragraph ends.

## 3. One instance, carried through the section

Pick one concrete, generic instance — no protagonist, no plot — and let it instantiate the whole point, rather than adding a new example for each sub-claim.

> Think of a coffee shop. What could go wrong? A wet floor could cause a slip. So they put down a caution sign and a non-slip mat, they show staff how to clean up spills quickly, and the manager keeps an eye out to make sure the mat is actually there and being used.

This is an **illustrative model**, not an anecdote. Test: does it have a plot? A coffee shop that generically has a wet floor does not. A specific worker on a specific day who slips and is rushed to hospital does — that's a narrated anecdote, and stays banned in data-led content. Illustrative models like the one above are permitted and encouraged — that is the whole distinction this test draws.

### 3a. Narrated instances — superseded, kept as a craft example

**This item no longer authorises a narrated anecdote in data-led content.** The plot test in §3 bans them without exception, which makes the permission below unreachable. The before/after pair is kept because it teaches gloss-in-place, sequencing and the stakes close, and those techniques transfer directly to an illustrative model. Read it for those; do not read it as permission.

The original rationale, for context: some abstract consequence-chains seem to need a named event to become legible rather than a generic model.

> **Before:** EHS matters because workplace and environmental harm reaches people first and the organization second. The consequences also arrive in sequence. An injury stops production, triggers a report to a regulator, and leads to an investigation. If the same hazard exists elsewhere, the corrective actions reach other sites too.
>
> **After:** These consequences also tend to arrive in a chain, one triggering the next. Picture a worker getting hurt on a machine. First, production stops. Then the company has to report the injury to a regulator (a government body that enforces safety rules). That report leads to an investigation. And if the same dangerous setup exists at the company's other locations, the fixes now have to be rolled out everywhere, not just where the accident happened. One injury in one building can end up reshaping how the whole company operates.

The after names an event ("a worker getting hurt"), sequences it (First... Then... That report leads to... And if...), glosses the jargon inline, and lands on a stakes sentence at the end rather than just closing the loop.

## 4. Gloss-in-place

Define a term of art inside the sentence that uses it, not in a separate glossary.

> permits (official permission to do it) and records (proof of what was done)
> a regulator (a government body that enforces safety rules)
> ergonomic strain — the wear a job puts on the body when the task doesn't fit the person doing it

## 5. Reader-language label, technical term subordinated

Put the plain description first; the technical term rides along as a parenthetical, not the headline.

> **Before:** Electrical energy, fire, explosion and pressure release.
> **After:** Energy that can burst out: electricity that can shock, fires and explosions, or pressure suddenly releasing from something like a tank or pipe.

## 6. Syntactic unpacking, not word substitution

This is the actual FKGL lever. Give every abstract subject an agent and a verb; split stacked clauses into separate sentences. Do not lower grade level by swapping words for "simpler" synonyms alone — see item 12 for why that can fail.

> **Before:** Organizations manage the three together because one activity can affect all of them.
> **After:** Companies manage the three together because one activity can affect all of them. A chemical spill can injure a worker, expose other employees to harmful vapor, and contaminate nearby water.

Splitting the stacked list into a second sentence with a concrete instance did more for readability than any word choice would have.

## 7. Label lands after the instance (for definitions, not illustrations)

For a category definition, give the instance first and let the label be the conclusion.

> A factory letting waste seep into a nearby stream is an environmental problem.

This differs from an example illustrating an already-stated abstraction, where the concept still comes first (see item 3's setup rule). Test which situation applies: is this sentence *defining* a category, or *illustrating* one already named?

## 8. Explicit contrast markers

Use However / On the other hand / But / So at beginner comprehension, including in third-person passages, where the prose would otherwise rely on unmarked juxtaposition.

## 9. Concrete sensory and temporal detail

> right there, at 2 p.m.
> the front gate
> a loose cable
> strain their back lifting a box

Small, specific, physical details make an abstract claim land as something real rather than something asserted.

## 10. Orienting heuristic before taxonomy

Before listing three or more categories, give the reader the question that sorts them.

> The easiest way to tell them apart? Ask who gets hurt, how, and how fast.

This is a decision procedure, not a classification — it tells the reader what to do with the categories, not just what they are.

---

## 11. No forward-referencing meta-commentary

Do not promise to explain something later. The next question-shaped H2 already signals what's coming.

> **Cut entirely:** That last phrase carries real weight, and we'll unpack it properly in the next section.
> **Replacement:** [nothing — the next paragraph states the scope directly, and the following H2's title does the signposting]

Flag and remove at draft time: "we'll unpack this later," "more on this below," "as we'll see," "we'll cover this."

## 12. The false-plain test

Before accepting a word swap as a simplification, ask: would a non-expert say this out loud to a friend explaining their job? A same-register synonym can fail this test as badly as the jargon it replaced.

> **Rejected as a "simpler" substitute:** stays in force
> **Actual plain word:** lasts

"Stays in force" is legal register in plain clothing. It is not simpler than the word it replaced; it just sounds less obviously technical. Test every substitution against the friend-explaining-their-job standard, not just against syllable count.

## 13. Iterative FKGL calibration, not one-shot fragmentation

Treat an FKGL target as a loop: cut, measure, check for over-fragmentation, adjust.

> One pass split every sentence into single clauses to chase a lower score and landed at FKGL 5.07 — technically "low enough," but choppy, because uniform short sentences are their own tell. Recombining lightly (rejoining two or three fragments per paragraph) brought it to 6.6–7.4 with better rhythm and the same vocabulary.

If one edit moves the score more than about 1.5 grades, check the sentence-length distribution before accepting the result.

## 14. Mechanism-completeness for conditional claims

An if/then sentence needs a concrete instance of how the trigger actually happens, not just a label for the consequence.

> **Before:** If the work could affect someone's safety, the duty reaches them too.
> **After:** Say a staff member mops the floor but doesn't put out a wet floor sign. A customer walking past could slip, even though they don't work there and never touched the mop. The risk came from the cafe's own work, not from anything the customer did, which is exactly why the duty reaches them too.

The before is grammatically complete and explains nothing. The after shows the mechanism, then states the same conclusion, which now actually follows from something.

## 15. Referential callback bridging

When two adjacent paragraphs are topically related but not causally connected, open the second with an explicit backward pointer to a specific noun from the first, not a generic transition. Distinct from contrast markers (item 8) — this is anaphoric callback, not logical opposition.

> **Before (disconnected):** ...so something like work stress counts too, not just physical injury. [paragraph break] The duty isn't a one-off box to tick when a business opens.
>
> **After (bridged):** ...so something like work stress counts too, not just physical injury. [paragraph break] None of this is a one-off box to tick when a business opens, though. A safe workplace today doesn't guarantee a safe workplace next month, which is why the duty lasts for as long as the work goes on. That means checking these same things stay true over time, not just setting them up once and hoping they hold.

"None of this" and "these same things" both point back to the specific list just given, closing the loop rather than starting a new one.

## Using this file

- Items 1–10 are calibrated against Kazi's original "What Is EHS?" draft.
- Items 11–15 are calibrated against live editing feedback during the PCBU responsibilities explainer.
- Items 2, 3 and 7 refine rules stated in `voice.md` (questions answered in their own paragraph, the plot test, concept-before-example). Those rules and this file agree; read them together.
- This file grows. Add new before/after pairs as they're found; do not restate existing items differently.
